messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

David, a man who had spent two decades helping others navigate the labyrinths of their own minds, now found himself utterly lost in his own. At fifty, he had built a respected psychology practice and a stable, loving marriage. Six months ago, at a professional conference out of state, that foundation had been shattered. After a networking dinner, he was assaulted and raped by a colleague in a hotel room. The attack was a blur of violence and humiliation, and he has been trying to outrun the memory of it ever since. The event itself remains a chaotic void in his mind, punctuated by the cloying smell of whiskey on the man’s breath and the sound of a distant ambulance siren that sliced through the night air after he finally escaped.

The memory, when it comes, never arrives as a story he can tell. Instead, it manifests as a visceral, wordless dread. He finds he cannot seem to put the frightening event into words, even in the privacy of his own thoughts. Sometimes, it’s just a wave of pure terror that washes over him with no accompanying image, leaving him breathless and shaking. On the rare occasions a fragment of a visual memory begins to form—the pattern on the hotel carpet, the glare of a bedside lamp—he feels an immediate, powerful urge to push it away before it can become whole, a mental flinching from a blow he knows is coming. When these memory fragments do surface, they serve only as brutal confirmation of what he has come to believe is an unchangeable truth: that he is no longer a person, but an object. This feeling of dehumanization is the most persistent and painful of his new convictions, reinforcing his belief that he is no longer capable of being the man, husband, or therapist he once was.

This conviction that he is irrevocably broken makes any attempt to piece together the event feel not just pointless, but dangerous. Because he feels like an object, contaminated and used, the memory is not a past event to be processed but a present-tense threat to be contained. He believes that to let it fully form would be to fully become that object again, and so he continues to block it, leaving it in its potent, nonverbal state. This sense of being fundamentally altered also leaves him perpetually on guard. He has become exquisitely sensitive to his surroundings, scanning for any sign of threat. The very feeling of being physically uncomfortable, even just sitting too long in his office chair, can send a jolt of alarm through him. He finds himself bracing for an impact that never comes, his world now a landscape of potential dangers.

This constant state of threat monitoring means that triggers are everywhere, and each one plunges him back into his darkest appraisals of himself. Last week, a siren screamed past his window during a session with a client. The sound was a physical shock, and in that instant, David was no longer a therapist in his chair but a thing, helpless and inert. The professional empathy he prided himself on vanished, replaced by a hollowed-out feeling, a sense that he was dead inside. He had to end the session early, claiming a sudden migraine, overwhelmed with the shame of his own incapacity. Even a walk home can be a minefield; the smell of alcohol from a passing bar or on someone’s breath is enough to make him feel his personhood dissolve, leaving only the sickening memory of being used.

Over the past few months, this vicious cycle has tightened its grip, systematically dismantling his life. He feels emotionally numb, a stranger to his own wife, who speaks of his distance with a growing sense of despair. His practice, once his calling, has become a place of profound dread. He is terrified that his clients will see through his carefully constructed professional facade to the broken man beneath. He has come to believe he is no longer capable of doing the work that once defined him. It was after cancelling a full day of appointments last Tuesday, unable to face the thought of sitting in a room with another person's pain while drowning in his own, that he finally sought help. He is terrified of losing everything, but what frightens him most is the quiet certainty that he has already become the hollow, incapable man he sees in his own reflection.
